extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative politics, and American democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the social, economic, geographic, and institutional factors that promote or undermine the durability of a federal union (illustrated by Tocqueville's analysis of the United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial extent and its dual effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “The extent of the country is then most prejudicial to the power of the State. But if the inhabitants of these vast regions are not divided by contrary interests, the extent of the territory may be favorable to their prosperity,”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large territorial size can harm unity when contrary interests arise among provinces (favoring dissension), but when inhabitants are not divided by opposing interests, large territory can be an advantage because a unified government promotes interregional exchange and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of government promotes economic interchange
rubrics_metrics.description: “The unity of the government promotes the interchange of the different productions of the soil, and increases their value by facilitating their consumption.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central political union that reduces internal barriers increases market size and mutual benefit between agricultural, commercial, and manufacturing regions — a key economic rationale for maintaining the union (illustrated by North/South/West complementarities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary regional economic interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct regional economies (South almost exclusively agricultural; North commercial and manufacturing; West both agricultural and manufacturing) create mutual interests that favor union because each region supplies goods and markets to the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union is sustained when regions are economically interdependent — e.g., North needs raw materials and cargoes from South/West; South/West need commercial resources and protection provided by the North.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on central commercial resources and naval protection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The South and the West ... stand in need of the commercial resources of the North. They are likewise interested in the maintenance of a powerful fleet by the Union, to protect them efficaciously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External defense (naval protection) and central commercial infrastructure are concrete common goods that bind otherwise different regions to remain in the federation; absence of these would make peripheral regions more vulnerable and independent-minded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common political opinions and legal-political principles
rubrics_metrics.description: From Maine to the Floridas ... the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. The same notions are entertained respecting liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, the jury, and the responsibility of the agents of Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared convictions about sovereignty, civil liberties, and institutions create cultural/political cohesion that underpins a lasting union; uniformity of such basic political beliefs is a stabilizing force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and moral-philosophical uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anglo-Americans acknowledge the absolute moral authority of the reason of the community ... and they hold that public opinion is the surest arbiter of what is lawful or forbidden, true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a large portion of the population accepts public opinion as arbiter and shares moral-philosophical views (perfectibility of man, faith in knowledge diffusion), social cohesion and compliance with shared norms strengthen the federation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective pride and perceived exceptionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anglo-Americans ... are separated from all other nations by a common feeling of pride ... convinced the inhabitants of the United States that they constitute the only religious, enlightened, and free people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shared national pride/exclusivist self-image can both unify internally and separate the polity from outsiders; this characteristic shapes attitudes toward governance and may influence cohesion positively or engender arrogance that affects external relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences of character and manners produced by slavery and climate
rubrics_metrics.description: “Slavery ... has modified the character and changed the habits of the natives of the South.” The Southern master is described as born to command; Northerners are more self-reliant, patient, and industrious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social institutions (slavery) and environmental factors produce divergent social habits and temperaments across regions. These character differences, even if not creating directly opposed material interests, produce tensions and misunderstandings that threaten union stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect threat of slavery via manners rather than direct opposing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: “Slavery, then, does not attack the American Union directly in its interests, but indirectly in its manners.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where economic interests align, entrenched social practices (like slavery) can alter elites' and citizens' dispositions (e.g., expectations of authority) in ways that undermine political solidarity and produce conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative strength and size of member states reduces unanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The greater the individual weakness of each of the contracting parties, the greater are the chances of the duration of the contract... But when one of the confederate States reckons ... it feels its own strength ... it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As constituent units grow in population, wealth, or territory they feel less dependent on the federal compact, seek greater influence, and may erode the unanimity or cooperative spirit necessary for durable federation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth and proliferation of states undermining coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid demographic and territorial expansion (doubling every ~22 years historically) increases the number and diversity of constituent polities and makes the continuance of a centralized federal government less likely over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncontrolled or rapid expansion multiplies actors with varying interests; a larger number of unequal states increases the chance of rivalry, envy, and fragmentation unless countervailing institutional mechanisms are effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and abruptness of social change as a destabilizer
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the changes which I have described were gradual ... the danger would be less; but the progress of society in America is precipitate, and almost revolutionary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid, revolutionary social and economic transformations compress generational turnover and produce sudden shifts in relative fortunes and political power, generating resentment and instability that endanger union continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic migration and shifting political center
rubrics_metrics.description: Westward population movement shifts the majority and the political center (e.g., basin of the Mississippi becoming the future centre of Federal Government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale migration alters the geographic basis of political power and representation, producing new majorities and longer distances between citizens and the federal capital; these changes affect policymaking and the perceived legitimacy of central institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal regional resources and natural harbors influencing economic divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Different natural features (e.g., northern ports with deep harbors vs. southern sandy, obstructed coasts) combined with laws (slavery) produce differential commercial and manufacturing development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geography plus institutional differences generate persistent economic asymmetries that feed divergent growth rates and political priorities among regions, which in turn affect their attitudes toward the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in representation and apportionment altering federal influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Censuses and apportionment routinely change the number of representatives per State (e.g., New York rising, Virginia falling), shifting congressional power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic re-apportionment based on population redistributes political weight among states, which can produce feelings of loss or domination and provoke political resistance or secessionist sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of relative deprivation and envy
rubrics_metrics.description: States that increase less rapidly look upon those more favored with envy and suspicion; the weak generally mistrust the justice and reason of the strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective perceptions of unfairness, even absent objective decline, can produce political agitation and threats to the union (e.g., tariff disputes perceived as favoring the North and injuring the South).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary modes of dissolution: secession or gradual atrophy of central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Union may, however, perish in two different ways: one of the confederate States may choose to retire ... or the authority of the Federal Government may be progressively entrenched on by the simultaneous tendency of the united republics to resume their independence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should distinguish between abrupt legal/constitutional rupture (secession) and slow abandonment of federal competencies (decentralization/inaction) as distinct failure modes with different early-warning signs and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller/weak constituent units more likely to adhere to union
rubrics_metrics.description: When in 1790 the most populous republics did not contain 500,000 inhabitants, each felt its own insignificance and compliance with federal authority was easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dependence produced by small size/weakness increases incentives to remain within a union for protection and markets; growth reduces that incentive and increases bargaining power and potential for withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political culture's hostility to centralization as a constraining factor
rubrics_metrics.description: “In America, centralization is by no means popular, and there is no surer means of courting the majority than by inveighing against the encroachments of the central power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A political culture that prizes local autonomy and mistrusts central power makes any trend toward consolidation politically costly and can be exploited rhetorically, limiting options for stronger federal action.
